prompt:
Pixel-art sprite sheet, single image, fully transparent background.

SUBJECT: the undead zombie basketball player in the attached reference image.
Match that character exactly: sickly grey-green skin, ragged mid-brown hair,
sunken eyes with small pale pupils, a lipless grin showing the teeth, dark
rotted patches on the arms and legs, a torn and ragged blue sleeveless
basketball jersey with a yellow number 13, torn blue shorts with white and
yellow trim, white high-top sneakers with blue and yellow flashes over white
socks. Identical colours, identical proportions, identical build and identical
height as the reference, in every frame.

LAYOUT: one horizontal row of 5 frames of equal width, evenly spaced. No
borders, no frame numbers, no labels, no background, no drop shadows.

CAMERA: locked off. Identical distance and eye level in every frame. The
character must be exactly the same height in every frame, and the same height
as in the reference image — do not zoom, crop, recompose or rescale between
frames. All frames share one ground line: the soles of the feet touch the same
horizontal line in every frame.

VIEW: front view, facing the viewer, squared to camera, low athletic stance
with the knees bent and the feet planted shoulder-width apart.

CRITICAL: exactly ONE hand dribbles — the hand nearer the RIGHT EDGE of the
picture, on the VIEWER'S RIGHT — in all four frames.

THE DRIBBLING HAND is flat and open: palm facing DOWN at the floor, fingers
spread and straight, the shape of a hand resting on the top of a ball. DRAW THE
SAME HAND FOUR TIMES — one drawing of that hand, the same shape, the same
spread of the fingers and the same angle to the floor, simply moved up and down
the picture from frame to frame. It travels in one straight line OUTSIDE HIS
HIP, further out from his centre line than his shoulder is, with clear
background showing between his forearm and his jersey.

THE HAND'S FOUR HEIGHTS, IN ORDER: in the LOWEST frame it is beside his KNEE,
overlapping the knee in the silhouette, with the hem of his shorts clearly
above his wrist; in the RISING frame it is level with the HEM of his shorts; in
the HIGHEST frame it is up at the WAISTBAND of his shorts, higher than it is in
any other frame; in the DRIVING DOWN frame it is back down to just BELOW the
hem. The HIGHEST frame is unmistakably the highest of the four and the LOWEST
frame unmistakably the lowest. Only in the LOWEST frame does the hand tilt a
little further down, at the end of the push.

THE FREE HAND IS NOT DRIBBLING AND DOES NOT COPY IT. That arm simply hangs:
upper arm against his ribs, elbow almost straight, and the hand hanging from
the wrist with the PALM TURNED IN toward his thigh, fingers straight, relaxed
and a little apart, pointing down at the floor. It is ONE DRAWING REPEATED IN
ALL FOUR FRAMES — the same shape and the same spread of the fingers every time
— held just clear of his leg so the whole hand shows against the background.
Both of his arms hang from the shoulders the way a living person's do, close to
his sides; the dribbling arm is the only one that reaches away from his body,
and it reaches DOWN.

This is a WHOLE-BODY action, not an arm action, and that is what makes it read
as weight. HIS WEIGHT SHIFTS ONTO THE LEG UNDER THE DRIBBLING HAND — the leg
nearer the RIGHT EDGE of the picture. As the hand goes down he leans that way
and settles onto that leg: THAT KNEE, the one nearer the RIGHT EDGE, is the one
that bends, and it bends deepest at the bottom of the push, coming forward over
its own shoe. That hip drops and that shoulder drops with it, so the SHOULDER
LINE TILTS. The far leg stays straighter and carries less of him. As the hand
comes up, that knee straightens again and his weight comes back toward the
middle.

HIS FEET ARE ONE DRAWING REPEATED IN ALL FOUR FRAMES: both shoes in the same
place on the floor, the same distance apart, at the same angle, as if traced
from one frame into the next three. THE GAP BETWEEN HIS SHOES IS THE SAME WIDTH
IN EVERY FRAME. He gets LOWER AND HIGHER BY BENDING AND STRAIGHTENING HIS
KNEES, never by spreading his feet or drawing them back in: the knee on the
dribbling side bends more deeply and comes forward over his toes as he sinks,
and straightens as he rises. His knees do all the work his feet are not allowed
to do.

HIS HEAD BARELY TRAVELS SIDEWAYS — it stays above his chest, and his face stays
turned to the viewer. What changes is its TILT, and only slightly: in the
LOWEST frame his head tips a little toward the dribbling side, the ear on that
side dropping toward that shoulder and the chin dipping; in the two middle
frames the tilt is about half of that; in the HIGHEST frame his head is level
and square to the camera, looking straight at the viewer. A slight tilt
throughout, never a full lean.

FRAMES, left to right:
1. CALIBRATION POSE: standing straight upright, feet shoulder-width apart, arms
   hanging relaxed at his sides, facing the viewer, in the plain neutral
   standing pose from the reference image. This exact pose appears as the first
   frame of every sheet in this set and must be drawn identically every time.
2. LOWEST, the push landed. His most compressed frame: both knees bent, and the
   knee nearer the RIGHT EDGE of the picture bent DEEPEST of the four frames,
   forward over its own shoe, with his weight plainly on that leg — that hip
   dropped and that shoulder dropped so the shoulder line is visibly tilted —
   and his shoes still exactly where they are in every other frame. His head is
   tilted a little toward the dribbling side, chin dipped. The dribbling arm is
   straight and the hand is at its lowest, overlapping his KNEE, wrist loose at
   the end of the follow-through. The free hand hangs at his side, swung
   slightly BEHIND him as he sinks.
3. RISING, and the HAND leads. The wrist bends back first and the hand has come
   up off the knee, elbow starting to fold. The body is still catching up: the
   dribbling shoulder is only beginning to lift, the knees are only beginning
   to straighten, and the head still carries about half its tilt. The torso
   visibly lags behind the hand. The free hand hangs at his side, swinging
   forward.
4. HIGHEST, his tallest and most open frame. His hand has reached the top of
   its travel, still out beyond his hip, elbow folded, ready to push down
   again. The shoulder line and the hips are level and the knees are at their
   straightest — still bent, still an athletic stance, and his shoes no further
   apart than in any other frame. His head is level and square to the camera,
   looking straight at the viewer. The free hand hangs at his side at the
   forward end of its swing.
5. DRIVING DOWN, and now the BODY leads. The KNEE nearer the RIGHT EDGE of the
   picture bends again and takes him down, his weight settling back onto that
   leg — that shoulder drops, that hip sinks, his shoes stay exactly where they
   are — and the head tilts halfway back toward the dribbling side, while the
   dribbling hand is still high, trailing behind. This frame is the one that
   sells the weight: the body has committed to the push and the hand has not
   caught up yet. The free hand hangs at his side, swinging back again.

This row is a seamless loop: frame 5 must flow back into frame 2 with no jump.

Everything above his feet — knees, hips, shoulders, spine, head — moves with
the dribble. The four frames must differ clearly BOTH in the height of the
dribbling hand AND in the tilt of the shoulder line.

STYLE: VGA-era 256-colour DOS-game pixel art, drawn pixel by pixel — NOT a
modern illustration with a pixel filter over it. The limits below are the look;
keep all of them: - At most THREE tones per material: a base, one darker
shadow, one lighter highlight. Hard edges between the tones. - NO gradients, NO
soft or airbrushed shading, NO glow, NO bloom, and NO anti-aliasing anywhere —
not on the outline, not between tones, not around the silhouette. - Where a
tone change needs softening, use visible ORDERED DITHER — a checkerboard of the
two tones. Dither, never blend. - Chunky square pixels on one consistent grid,
plainly visible at full size. - A bold dark outline around the silhouette and
around the major forms inside it. The background must be fully transparent
(alpha 0) with no haze, glow or soft fringe around the silhouette. Output a
wide landscape image.

The character is NOT holding a basketball in any frame — the ball is drawn
separately by the game.
